title: He Was Last After Six Rounds. Then Praggnanandhaa Won Four Straight and Made History in Oslo.
excerpt: The 20-year-old from Chennai became the first Indian to win Norway Chess, beating Magnus Carlsen twice in classical play. World champion Gukesh finished last.
body:
The scoreboard after Round 6 of Norway Chess 2026 read like a slow funeral for Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu. The 20-year-old Indian grandmaster sat sixth and last in the six-player elite field, 6.5 points behind tournament leader Wesley So. Two classical defeats in a row — to So and then to Alireza Firouzja — had left him all but mathematically eliminated.

Then something extraordinary happened. Praggnanandhaa won four consecutive classical games to close the tournament — a streak no one in the field could match — and finished on 18 points, one clear of So, to become the first Indian player ever to win Norway Chess.

## The Carlsen Double

The headline within the headline was the Carlsen factor. Praggnanandhaa beat Magnus Carlsen — the world’s highest-rated player and five-time world champion — not once but twice in classical time control during the tournament, a feat that no other active player can claim in a single elite event this year.

The first classical win came in Round 5, a grinding positional squeeze that saw Carlsen outmanoeuvred in a queenless middlegame. The second, in Round 8, was more emphatic — Praggnanandhaa held the black pieces and dismantled Carlsen’s King’s Indian setup with precision that left the Norwegian grandmaster visibly frustrated.



> **"“It’s more important for the tournament that I get this win than thinking that it’s Magnus,” Praggnanandhaa said after his Round 8 victory."**


“It’s more important for the tournament that I get this win than thinking that it’s Magnus,” Praggnanandhaa said after his Round 8 victory. “Of course, it’s great to do it against Magnus, but I think winning any game at this stage of the tournament is good.”

## Gukesh’s Quiet Struggle

The other Indian story from Oslo was less celebratory. World champion Gukesh Dommaraju finished last in the standings on 8 points, suffering three classical defeats — to Carlsen, Firouzja, and Vincent Keymer — and managing only one classical win in the entire tournament.

Since winning the World Championship title in December 2024, Gukesh has struggled to replicate that form at elite invitationals. He withdrew from the full Grand Chess Tour earlier this year to focus on training ahead of his title defence against Uzbekistan’s Javokhir Sindarov, who won the Candidates Tournament in Cyprus.

The contrast between India’s two prodigies — one ascending, the other recalibrating — captures a broader truth about chess at the highest level. The crown sits heavy. Praggnanandhaa, unburdened by a title to defend, played with the freedom of someone with nothing to lose and everything to gain.

## The Final Standings

The tournament concluded with Praggnanandhaa on 18 points, So on 17, Firouzja third on 15.5, and Carlsen fourth on 13. In the women’s section, Kazakhstan’s Bibisara Assaubayeva claimed the title, while India’s Divya Deshmukh and Koneru Humpy finished fifth and sixth respectively.

## India’s Chess Golden Age

For the diaspora, Praggnanandhaa’s triumph is another data point in what can only be described as India’s chess golden age. The country now holds the world championship (Gukesh), the Norway Chess title (Praggnanandhaa), and the Women’s Candidates winner (Vaishali Rameshbabu, Praggnanandhaa’s elder sister). Arjun Erigaisi remains in the world’s top five. The Candidates challenger is Sindarov, not an Indian — but the depth chart suggests the next one could well be.

In Indian-American communities, where chess academies have proliferated since Viswanathan Anand’s era, Praggnanandhaa’s win in Oslo is both validation and inspiration. The 20-year-old from Chennai has announced himself as a force that the game’s establishment can no longer ignore.

*Sources: FIDE, Chess.com, ChessBase, The Indian Eye*
